provenance: Editorial intermediate TOPIK II Level 3 selection; not an official per-level grammar checklist; educator review required.

grammarPoints.title: -다가
grammarPoints.hint: An action is interrupted by another or takes an unexpected turn.
grammarPoints.description: An action is interrupted by another or takes an unexpected turn. It marks an activity that was already underway before another event interrupted or changed it.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 다가 to an action stem, then describe the interruption or change.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 책을 읽다가 잠들었어요. — I fell asleep while reading. 읽다가 shows that reading was still in progress when sleep intervened.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Ordinary -고 often joins completed actions; -다가 highlights an interrupted activity.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I fell asleep while reading.
I met a friend on my way home.

cards.englishHint: I stopped studying to rest.
I fell while walking.
I answered the phone while working.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 놓다
grammarPoints.hint: An action is completed and its result is deliberately left ready.
grammarPoints.description: An action is completed and its result is deliberately left ready. It emphasizes that someone deliberately leaves the completed action's result in place.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use the verb's 아/어 form, then 놓다: 열다 → 열어 놓다.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 창문을 열어 놓았어요. — I opened the window and left it open. 열어 놓았어요 means the window was opened and kept open afterward.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not equate with ordinary past: 열었어요 does not necessarily mean left open.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I opened the window and left it open.
I booked the room in advance.

cards.englishHint: I closed the door and left it closed.
I found the materials and kept them ready.
I prepared the food ahead of time.

grammarPoints.title: Passive verb forms: 열리다 / 닫히다
grammarPoints.hint: Korean passive verbs describe a change or action from the perspective of what is affected, often without saying who did it.
grammarPoints.description: Korean passive verbs describe a change or action from the perspective of what is affected, often without saying who did it. Some common verbs have paired active and passive forms.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Stem / noun as specified] + Passive verb forms: 열리다 / 닫히다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Learn common active/passive pairs instead of mechanically attaching a suffix to every verb: 열다 → 열리다, 닫다 → 닫히다, 잡다 → 잡히다, 보다 → 보이다. Conjugate the resulting passive verb normally.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 문이 열렸어요. — The door opened. 문이 열렸어요 describes the door as the thing that opened or was opened, while 누가 문을 열었어요 focuses on the person opening it.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Passive morphology is not freely predictable for every verb. Not every -이/-히/-리/-기 spelling marks a passive, and some pairs are lexicalized.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The door opened.
The window was closed.

cards.englishHint: The ball was caught.
The picture is easy to see.
The sound can be heard.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어지다 (passive / spontaneous result)
grammarPoints.hint: Some verbs combine with -아/어지다 to show an action happening to something or a result occurring without naming an agent.
grammarPoints.description: Some verbs combine with -아/어지다 to show an action happening to something or a result occurring without naming an agent. Other uses indicate a gradual change in state.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Choose a verb that permits this construction, form its 아/어 stem, then attach 지다: 지우다 → 지워지다, 쓰다 → 써지다. In the past: 지워졌어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 글씨가 지워졌어요. — The writing was erased. 글씨가 지워졌어요 says the writing was erased, focusing on its result rather than the person doing the erasing.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -아/어지다 is not a universal passive marker. Compare 추워졌어요 ('became cold') with 지워졌어요 ('was erased'); not every verb forms a natural passive this way.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The writing was erased.
This sentence is easy to write.

cards.englishHint: The name doesn't stick in my memory.
The writing erases easily.
The sentence came out well.

grammarPoints.title: Causative verb pairs: 먹이다 / 재우다
grammarPoints.hint: Causative verbs make another person or thing perform an action or enter a state: feeding someone, putting a child to sleep, or dressing someone.
grammarPoints.description: Causative verbs make another person or thing perform an action or enter a state: feeding someone, putting a child to sleep, or dressing someone. Because many forms are lexicalized, learners need to practice individual verb pairs and the roles their sentences assign.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Stem / noun as specified] + Causative verb pairs: 먹이다 / 재우다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Learn common lexicalized causative pairs and their particle patterns: 먹다 → 먹이다, 자다 → 재우다, 입다 → 입히다. The person affected may take 을/를 or 에게 depending on the verb.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 엄마가 아기에게 밥을 먹여요. — Mom feeds the baby rice. 엄마가 아기에게 밥을 먹여요 has the mother cause the baby to eat; 먹여요 is the causative of 먹다.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not add -이/-히/-리/-기 blindly to any verb. The permitted form and whether the causee takes 을/를 or 에게 depend on the verb.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Mom feeds the baby rice.
Dad puts the child to sleep.

cards.englishHint: Mom dresses the child.
Dad wakes the baby.
The teacher seats the student.

grammarPoints.title: -게 하다 (make / let someone do)
grammarPoints.hint: Use -게 하다 to say that someone causes, instructs or allows another person to do an action.
grammarPoints.description: Use -게 하다 to say that someone causes, instructs or allows another person to do an action. It is productive even where there is no convenient lexical causative verb.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Stem / noun as specified] + -게 하다 (make / let someone do)

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 게 하다 to the action stem, then conjugate 하다: 읽다 → 읽게 하다 → 읽게 했어요. The person directed to act often takes 에게/한테.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 선생님이 학생들에게 책을 읽게 했어요. — The teacher made the students read books. 선생님이 학생들에게 책을 읽게 했어요 means the teacher made or had the students read, rather than reading to them.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: The same surface form can express permission or influence depending on context. Contrast a lexical causative such as 재우다 with 재우게 하다.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The teacher made the students read books.
Mom made the child do homework.

cards.englishHint: The doctor had the patient walk.
The teacher had me present.
The parents let the child rest.

grammarPoints.title: -게 하다 (cause a state)
grammarPoints.hint: The same -게 하다 structure can make someone or something become a particular way, such as happy, sad, anxious or comfortable.
grammarPoints.description: The same -게 하다 structure can make someone or something become a particular way, such as happy, sad, anxious or comfortable. This uses a descriptive stem.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Stem / noun as specified] + -게 하다 (cause a state)

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 게 하다 to the descriptive stem: 기쁘다 → 기쁘게 하다; 슬프다 → 슬프게 하다. The subject or event causes the resulting state.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 그 말이 저를 기쁘게 했어요. — Those words made me happy. 그 말이 저를 기쁘게 했어요 says those words caused me to feel happy, rather than that I chose to become happy.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: An action causing another person to DO something and an event causing a person to FEEL something use similar forms but different complements.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Those words made me happy.
That film made me sad.

cards.englishHint: That song makes me happy.
That news surprised everyone.
Those words made my friend angry.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 가다 / 오다
grammarPoints.hint: An action or change continues onward, or has progressed toward the present.
grammarPoints.description: An action or change continues onward, or has progressed toward the present. Use 가다 for change continuing away from the present and 오다 for change continuing toward the present.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 가다 or 오다 after an 아/어 verb form; 가다 looks forward, 오다 looks back.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 조금씩 한국어를 배워 가고 있어요. — I'm gradually learning Korean. 배워 가고 있어요 says that the learning continues from this point onward.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: These are not literal movement verbs in this construction; the time perspective matters.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I'm gradually learning Korean.
I've studied up to this point.

cards.englishHint: I'll continue making an effort.

cards.fullSentence: 지난 몇 년 동안 변해 왔어요.
cards.englishHint: It has changed over the past several years.
Technology continues to advance.

grammarPoints.title: -는 동안
grammarPoints.hint: Another action happens during the span of time that an activity is underway.
grammarPoints.description: Another action happens during the span of time that an activity is underway. It describes the time span during which another event or action occurs.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 는 to the first action stem, then 동안, then say what happens during it.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 제가 요리하는 동안 동생이 청소했어요. — While I cooked, my sibling cleaned. 요리하는 동안 frames the time during which the sibling cleaned.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Unlike -(으)면서, the two clauses may involve different people doing the actions.

lessonExamples.englishHint: While I cooked, my sibling cleaned.
I kept my phone off during class.

cards.englishHint: I read while the child slept.
I listened to music while waiting.

cards.fullSentence: 제가 없는 동안 집을 봐 주세요.
cards.englishHint: Please watch the house while I'm away.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다
grammarPoints.hint: Something tends to be true or falls on one side of a range, without being absolute.
grammarPoints.description: Something tends to be true or falls on one side of a range, without being absolute. It expresses a general tendency rather than a firm, absolute claim.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For actions use -는 편이다; for present descriptions use -(으)ㄴ 편이다.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 일찍 일어나는 편이에요. — I tend to wake up early. 일어나는 편이에요 means getting up early is a usual tendency, not an everyday certainty.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use it for precise counts, and choose action versus adjective modifiers correctly.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I tend to wake up early.
This restaurant is relatively cheap.

cards.englishHint: Our neighborhood is rather quiet.
I tend to exercise often.
This test is on the difficult side.

grammarPoints.title: -고 싶어 하다 (someone else's wishes)
grammarPoints.hint: To describe another person's visible or reported wish, Korean commonly uses -고 싶어 하다 rather than speaking as though you directly know their inner feelings.
grammarPoints.description: To describe another person's visible or reported wish, Korean commonly uses -고 싶어 하다 rather than speaking as though you directly know their inner feelings. It is especially useful when reporting what friends, family members or other people want to do.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Stem / noun as specified] + -고 싶어 하다 (someone else's wishes)

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 고 싶어 하다 to the action verb stem, then conjugate 하다: 가다 → 가고 싶어 해요, 먹다 → 먹고 싶어 해요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 동생은 놀고 싶어 해요. — My younger sibling wants to play. 동생은 놀고 싶어 해요 reports the younger sibling's wish to play, using 싶어 해요 for a third person's desire.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: For your own desire, -고 싶어요 is natural. Don't force -고 싶어 하다 for the speaker's own straightforward wishes.

lessonExamples.englishHint: My younger sibling wants to play.
My friend wants to go to Korea.

cards.englishHint: The child wants to sleep more.
Minsu wants to watch a movie.
My sibling wants to play a game.

grammarPoints.title: -나 보다 / -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (seems likely)
grammarPoints.hint: Use these endings to infer a situation from what you can see or hear, without claiming certainty.
grammarPoints.description: Use these endings to infer a situation from what you can see or hear, without claiming certainty. Choice of form is affected by action versus descriptive verb.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Stem / noun as specified] + -나 보다 / -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (seems likely)

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Action verb stems commonly use -나 보다 (오다 → 오나 봐요); descriptive verbs take -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (바쁘다 → 바쁜가 봐요). Some common variation exists.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 밖에 비가 오나 봐요. — It seems to be raining outside. 밖에 비가 오나 봐요 expresses a guess based on visible or audible clues that it is raining.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not confuse this with direct eyewitness recollection -더라고요 or a simple future prediction -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요.

lessonExamples.englishHint: It seems to be raining outside.
My friend seems busy.

cards.englishHint: It looks like someone is home.
That person seems tired.
It looks like the bus is coming soon.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 보이다
grammarPoints.hint: Something appears a certain way to the speaker, who is describing an impression.
grammarPoints.description: Something appears a certain way to the speaker, who is describing an impression. It reports how something appears to the observer, rather than what it definitively is.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 보이다 after a descriptive verb's 아/어 form: 피곤하다 → 피곤해 보이다.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 오늘 피곤해 보여요. — You look tired today. 피곤해 보여요 describes an observed appearance, not proof the listener feels tired.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This 보이다 is different from -아/어 보다, which asks someone to try an action.

lessonExamples.englishHint: You look tired today.
The clothes look warm.

cards.englishHint: That person looks busy.
The food looks delicious.
The expression looks sad.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다
grammarPoints.hint: A future or uncertain possibility: 'it might happen' or 'it may be true'.
grammarPoints.description: A future or uncertain possibility: 'it might happen' or 'it may be true'. It leaves open the possibility of an uncertain outcome.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use the verb's -(으)ㄹ form, followed by 지도 몰라요: 오다 → 올지도 몰라요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 내일 비가 올지도 몰라요. — It might rain tomorrow. 올지도 몰라요 makes the forecast uncertain instead of stating a definite expectation.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is weaker than the confident prediction in -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

lessonExamples.englishHint: It might rain tomorrow.
That person might know too.

cards.englishHint: The train might be late.
The story might be true.
It might be harder than expected.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 텐데
grammarPoints.hint: An expectation offered as background for concern, contrast, or advice.
grammarPoints.description: An expectation offered as background for concern, contrast, or advice. It supplies an expectation that can lead into a worry, suggestion or contrasting reality.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add -(으)ㄹ to the predicate stem and then the separate word 텐데.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 밖이 추울 텐데 따뜻하게 입으세요. — It will probably be cold, so dress warmly. 추울 텐데 predicts cold weather and supplies the reason for the clothing advice.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is not just future tense; the following clause tells why the prediction matters.

lessonExamples.englishHint: It will probably be cold, so dress warmly.
If we leave now, we'll probably be late.

cards.englishHint: It'll likely be hard alone, so I'll help.
Traffic will likely be bad, so take the subway.
You'll probably be busy; is that okay?

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 테니까
grammarPoints.hint: A speaker's promise or strong prediction that supports advice or a request.
grammarPoints.description: A speaker's promise or strong prediction that supports advice or a request. The speaker gives their expectation as the reason for the next advice or request.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add -(으)ㄹ 테니까 to the stem, then say what the listener should do.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 제가 준비할 테니까 먼저 가세요. — I'll prepare things, so please go ahead. 준비할 테니까 commits the speaker to preparing, justifying 'go ahead'.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use it as a generic because; intentions or expectations drive the reason.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I'll prepare things, so please go ahead.
It will likely rain, so take an umbrella.

cards.englishHint: I'll contact you, so please wait.
The food will cool, so eat now.
I'll pay, so don't worry.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다
grammarPoints.hint: An event almost happened, but the result was avoided: a close call.
grammarPoints.description: An event almost happened, but the result was avoided: a close call. It refers to something that nearly happened but ultimately did not.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use -(으)ㄹ with the stem followed by 뻔했어요 for a past near miss.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 버스를 놓칠 뻔했어요. — I almost missed the bus. 놓칠 뻔했어요 means the speaker nearly missed the bus but did not.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: The expression does not say the bad event actually happened; don't treat it as completed past.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I almost missed the bus.
I nearly fell on the stairs.

cards.englishHint: I nearly forgot the appointment.
I nearly took the wrong road.
I nearly lost my phone.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어야겠다
grammarPoints.hint: Realizing or deciding 'I really should' do something now or soon.
grammarPoints.description: Realizing or deciding 'I really should' do something now or soon. It describes reaching a decision or realizing what one should do.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Take the verb stem, add 아야/어야 and then 겠어요: 가다 → 가야겠어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 이제 운동해야겠어요. — I really should exercise now. 운동해야겠어요 signals a new personal decision to exercise.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Obligation -아/어야 해요 may come from outside; -아/어야겠다 stresses realization or resolve.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I really should exercise now.
I should wake up early tomorrow.

cards.englishHint: I should rest today.
I should call my parents.
I should reread this book.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다
grammarPoints.hint: Knowing or not knowing how to perform an action or learned skill.
grammarPoints.description: Knowing or not knowing how to perform an action or learned skill. It can express knowing or not knowing how to do an action; context determines the nuance.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add -(으)ㄹ to the verb stem, then 줄 알아요 or 줄 몰라요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 수영할 줄 알아요. — I know how to swim. 수영할 줄 알아요 reports learned knowledge of swimming, not permission to swim.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 also expresses ability but may refer to circumstances rather than learned know-how.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I know how to swim.
My sibling doesn't know how to ride a bike.

cards.englishHint: My father knows how to cook.
I don't know how to drive.
My friend knows how to play the piano.

grammarPoints.title: -자마자
grammarPoints.hint: Something happens immediately after another event, almost without a gap.
grammarPoints.description: Something happens immediately after another event, almost without a gap. The second event follows immediately after the first, with essentially no gap.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 자마자 straight to the preceding verb stem, then state the next event.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 집에 오자마자 잠들었어요. — I fell asleep as soon as I got home. 오자마자 marks arriving home as the point immediately preceding sleep.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Unlike -고 나서, this emphasizes that almost no time passes between actions.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I fell asleep as soon as I got home.
I left as soon as class ended.

cards.englishHint: I laughed as soon as I answered.
The cat left as soon as I opened the door.
I contacted them as soon as I heard.

grammarPoints.title: -도록 (purpose)
grammarPoints.hint: A goal is expressed so that someone can act to make that result happen.
grammarPoints.description: A goal is expressed so that someone can act to make that result happen. It gives the goal the first action aims to achieve.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 도록 to the first verb stem; the second clause gives the action aimed at the goal.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 잊지 않도록 메모하세요. — Write it down so you don't forget. 잊지 않도록 is the goal 'so as not to forget', and taking a note is the means.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -도록 also marks time limits in other contexts, but this point tests purpose.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Write it down so you don't forget.
Speak up so everyone can hear.

cards.englishHint: Leave early so you won't be late.
Let everyone know about it.
Check so you don't make a mistake.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ수록
grammarPoints.hint: Two quantities or tendencies change together: 'the more..., the more...'.
grammarPoints.description: Two quantities or tendencies change together: 'the more..., the more...'. One quantity or quality changes in proportion to another.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 을수록 to most consonant stems, ㄹ수록 to vowel stems, and keep it attached.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 연습할수록 쉬워져요. — The more I practice, the easier it gets. 연습할수록 says that additional practice corresponds to greater ease.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -(으)면 only means 'if/when'; -수록 adds the idea of increasing degree.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The more I practice, the easier it gets.
The more I know, the more interesting it is.

cards.englishHint: The more I read, the more I like it.
The more I think, the stranger it seems.
As time passes, it gets colder.

grammarPoints.title: -다 보니까
grammarPoints.hint: Continuing or repeating an activity produces an eventual discovery or result.
grammarPoints.description: Continuing or repeating an activity produces an eventual discovery or result. A repeated or continued activity leads the speaker to discover a result.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 다 보니까 to an action stem, then describe the result that developed.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 매일 걷다 보니까 체력이 좋아졌어요. — Walking every day improved my stamina. 걷다 보니까 tells us repeated walking led to an improved level of stamina.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: A single one-time event usually doesn't give the sense of repeated experience this needs.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Walking every day improved my stamina.
As I studied, Korean became fun.

cards.englishHint: I kept working and it got late.
After listening repeatedly, I understood.
We became close by meeting often.

grammarPoints.title: -느라고
grammarPoints.hint: Being busy doing one action results in inconvenience or missing another action.
grammarPoints.description: Being busy doing one action results in inconvenience or missing another action. It gives a reason while highlighting that the first action prevented another action.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 느라고 to an action verb stem; a negative or inconvenient result usually follows.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 숙제하느라고 전화를 못 받았어요. — I couldn't answer because of homework. 숙제하느라고 explains why the speaker could not answer the phone.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Usually the same person performs both clauses. It is not interchangeable with every 'because'.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I couldn't answer because of homework.
I slept late because I was working.

cards.englishHint: I couldn't call because I was driving.
Cleaning left me with no time.
I was busy preparing for the exam.

grammarPoints.title: -는 바람에
grammarPoints.hint: An unforeseen or unwelcome event causes another negative outcome.
grammarPoints.description: An unforeseen or unwelcome event causes another negative outcome. It presents an unexpected or inconvenient event as the cause of a result.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use -는 바람에 for an unfolding action, or -(으)ㄴ 바람에 for a completed event.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 비가 오는 바람에 소풍이 취소됐어요. — The picnic was cancelled due to rain. 비가 오는 바람에 connects unexpected rain to cancellation of the picnic.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: A helpful cause is more naturally expressed with 덕분에; 바람에 typically conveys misfortune.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The picnic was cancelled due to rain.
I was late because the bus arrived late.

cards.fullSentence: 갑자기 정전되는 바람에 일을 못 했어요.
cards.englishHint: I couldn't work because of a blackout.
I was late because of traffic.

cards.fullSentence: 컴퓨터가 고장 나는 바람에 자료를 잃었어요.
cards.englishHint: I lost my data because my computer broke.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ/는 덕분에
grammarPoints.hint: Credit a person or situation for a positive result: 'thanks to'.
grammarPoints.description: Credit a person or situation for a positive result: 'thanks to'. It credits a person or situation with producing a beneficial outcome.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use -는 for a present action or -(으)ㄴ for a completed action before 덕분에.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구가 도와준 덕분에 끝냈어요. — I finished thanks to my friend. 도와준 덕분에 says the friend's help is the reason the task was finished.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: For a bad consequence, use a different causal phrase rather than praising it with 덕분에.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I finished thanks to my friend.
I understood thanks to the teacher.

cards.englishHint: I succeeded thanks to my family.
My skill improved thanks to practice.
Leaving early got me there on time.

grammarPoints.title: -는 대신에
grammarPoints.hint: One action is done instead of another; it can also signal a trade-off.
grammarPoints.description: One action is done instead of another; it can also signal a trade-off. It proposes one action in place of another, or an alternative arrangement.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 는 대신에 to an action verb stem and describe the replacement.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 택시를 타는 대신에 걸었어요. — I walked instead of taking a taxi. 타는 대신에 says walking replaced taking the taxi in this example.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is an explicit substitution; -거나 simply lists alternatives without choosing a replacement.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I walked instead of taking a taxi.
I cooked rather than eating out.

cards.englishHint: I read instead of watching a movie.
I drank water instead of tea.
I went to bed early rather than late.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ/는 반면에
grammarPoints.hint: Present contrasting sides of a situation: 'whereas' or 'on the other hand'.
grammarPoints.description: Present contrasting sides of a situation: 'whereas' or 'on the other hand'. It places two aspects side by side to highlight a difference.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use -는 before 반면에 for actions, or -(으)ㄴ for descriptive verbs.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 형은 조용한 반면에 저는 활발해요. — My brother is quiet, whereas I am lively. 조용한 반면에 contrasts the brother's quiet nature with the speaker's lively nature.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Unlike a simple sequence, this construction explicitly compares two properties or outcomes.

lessonExamples.englishHint: My brother is quiet, whereas I am lively.

lessonExamples.fullSentence: 이 집은 작은 반면에 위치가 좋아요.
lessonExamples.englishHint: This home is small, but well located.

cards.fullSentence: 버스는 싼 반면에 시간이 오래 걸려요.
cards.englishHint: The bus is cheap but takes a long time.

cards.fullSentence: 언니는 운동을 좋아하는 반면에 저는 독서를 좋아해요.
cards.englishHint: My sister likes sports, but I prefer reading.
I'm free on weekends but busy on weekdays.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ/는지 알다/모르다
grammarPoints.hint: Embed a question inside 'know' or 'don't know', without ending the clause as a direct question.
grammarPoints.description: Embed a question inside 'know' or 'don't know', without ending the clause as a direct question. The speaker embeds an unknown fact or question inside another sentence.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use -는지 for present action verbs or -(으)ㄴ지 for descriptive verbs, then 알아요/몰라요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 그가 어디에 사는지 몰라요. — I don't know where he lives. 사는지 몰라요 means 'don't know where he lives', making the question the object of knowledge.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not place a full direct question ending inside the clause; formation depends on verb type.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I don't know where he lives.
Do you know whether the food is spicy?

cards.englishHint: I don't know when it starts.
I don't know why that is.
Do you know which road is faster?

grammarPoints.title: -던
grammarPoints.hint: A remembered past action that was ongoing or happened repeatedly, used before a noun.
grammarPoints.description: A remembered past action that was ongoing or happened repeatedly, used before a noun. It recalls something witnessed, repeated or unfinished in the past.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 던 to an action verb stem, then put the noun it describes after it.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 어릴 때 살던 집을 찾았어요. — I found the house I lived in as a child. 살던 집 recalls a house the speaker used to live in over a stretch of time.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Compare -았/었던, which often views a prior event as completed; -던 foregrounds remembered duration.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I found the house I lived in as a child.
Where is the book I was reading?

cards.englishHint: The shop I used to visit closed.
I remember the food Mom used to make.
I continued the drama I had been watching.

grammarPoints.title: -았/었던
grammarPoints.hint: A past action or state remembered as completed, often unlike the present situation.
grammarPoints.description: A past action or state remembered as completed, often unlike the present situation. It typically recalls a past action as completed and looks back on it now.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use the past 아/어 form plus 던: 읽다 → 읽었던, 가다 → 갔던.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 어제 읽었던 책이에요. — It's the book I read yesterday. 읽었던 책 places the book inside an experience of reading already completed.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -던 can recall an interrupted or habitual past, while -았/었던 emphasizes a completed past event.

lessonExamples.englishHint: It's the book I read yesterday.
It's the neighborhood I used to live in.

cards.englishHint: It's the restaurant I went to last year.
It's someone I met last time.
It's a song I liked as a child.

grammarPoints.title: -더라고요 (what I found firsthand)
grammarPoints.hint: Use -더라고요 to tell someone about something you noticed or experienced firsthand and are now recalling.
grammarPoints.description: Use -더라고요 to tell someone about something you noticed or experienced firsthand and are now recalling. It often conveys a discovery rather than a general claim.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Stem / noun as specified] + -더라고요 (what I found firsthand)

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 더라고요 to the relevant verb or descriptive stem when reporting past observation: 맛있다 → 맛있더라고요, 춥다 → 춥더라고요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 그 식당 음식이 맛있더라고요. — I found that restaurant's food tasty. 그 식당 음식이 맛있더라고요 tells the listener that the speaker personally found the restaurant's food tasty.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: It is not just the ordinary past tense. The form generally points to the speaker's own observation, and its person/tense restrictions require care.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I found that restaurant's food tasty.
It turned out to be cold outside yesterday.

cards.englishHint: I found the movie really interesting.
The café was quiet when I went.
I noticed that person speaks Korean well.
